title: Six Core Human Needs · Know Your Drive
vimeoName: 7. Six Core human needs - Know your drive

segments.text: By now, you've learned the six human needs: certainty, variety,
significance, love and connection, growth, and contribution.
These needs influence all of us, and they don't disappear when you come to work.
They influence how you respond to change, how you communicate, what motivates you,
and what frustrates you. The more you understand what drives you, the more choice
you have in how you respond. Let's start with certainty.
At work, certainty can mean wanting clear expectations, reliable systems, and
knowing what success looks like. But when certainty becomes too important, change
can feel threatening. A new process, a different schedule, a new way of
doing something. Instead of asking, "Why are we changing this?" ask,
"What do I need to understand so I can adapt?" You can create certainty through
preparation, communication, organization, and skill.
Then there is variety. Some people love new problems, new projects, and different
tasks. That can bring creativity and energy to a team.
But too much variety can become distraction, starting lots of things, getting bored
with routine, or changing a process before it has had time to work.
Ask yourself, "How can I create healthy challenge without creating unnecessary
chaos?" Learn something new, improve a process.
But remember, not everything needs to change just because change feels exciting.
Significance is the need to feel that we matter.
At work, this can mean wanting recognition, responsibility, or knowing that your
work has value. You can seek significance by needing credit, proving yourself,
or needing to be right, or you can meet it through excellence, reliability,
solving problems, and making a contribution that genuinely matters.
Instead of asking, "Do people notice me?" ask, "Am I creating value?"
Connection is also a powerful need.
Most of us want to feel that we belong and that people respect us.
Healthy connection is built through trust, listening, helping each other,
showing appreciation, and communicating honestly.
But the need for connection can make us avoid difficult conversations.
We may stay quiet because we don't want someone to be upset with us.
Real connection does not mean agreeing all the time.
Strong teams can disagree and still respect one another.
Growth is the need to learn and become more capable.
At work, this might mean learning a new skill, asking for feedback, improving
how you communicate, or becoming better at something you already do.
When work feels repetitive, ask, "What can I learn from this?
What can I become better at?" Growth does not always have to come from someone
else. It is something you can take ownership of. And finally, contribution.
Contribution is the need to give beyond ourselves.
At work, it can be as simple as helping someone, sharing what you know, improving a
process for the next person, or solving a problem before it becomes someone else's
problem. Contribution changes the question from, "What am I getting from this?"
to, "What am I adding?" And that shift can change the experience of work.
None of these needs are good or bad. What matters is how we choose to meet them.
Certainty can make you prepared or resistant to change.
Variety can make you creative or distracted.
Significance can lead to excellence or ego.
Connection can build trust or make you afraid to speak honestly.
Growth can make you curious and capable.
Contribution can turn work into something bigger than yourself.
Think about your own work. Which two needs influence you most?
How do they help you, and how might they sometimes get in your way?
Then ask, "What is a healthier way I can meet this need while also helping the
team?" Self-awareness gives you choice.
You cannot always control what happens around you, but you can understand what
drives you, choose how you respond, and use your needs in a way that helps you grow
and helps the people around you grow too.
